extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners (litigators, prosecutors), IP counsel, courts
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and case-law examples on assessing patent-eligibility under 35 U.S.C. §101 (Alice framework), focusing on what makes claims 'directed to an abstract idea' and whether they contain an 'inventive concept.' Compiles recurring standards courts used to find claims ineligible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Directed to an abstract idea
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts repeatedly find claims 'directed to' an abstract idea (e.g., communication between customer and business, transferring settings, teaching, fundamental commercial transactions, organizing information, bookmarking, collecting and transmitting vehicle data, report generation, business intelligence, payment processing, comparing collections of information, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples across cases: grouping movies by combination categories, using viewing history to recommend content, lending books for a limited time (electronic book as digital equivalent), connecting buyers and sellers, keeping a nutritional log, encoding/decoding data, collecting copies of business-process information and storing them centrally. If the claimed concept has clear pre-computer analogs or is a longstanding human practice, courts will treat it as an abstract idea.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lack of inventive concept
rubrics_metrics.description: Even if a claim is directed to an abstract idea, it must include an 'inventive concept' — additional limitations that transform the idea into patent-eligible subject matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts routinely find no inventive concept where the claims merely apply the abstract idea using generic computer, telephonic, or network components, routine or well‑understood activity, or conventional implementation. The inventive-concept inquiry looks for meaningful limitations beyond the abstract idea itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generic computer components insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: Recitation of generic hardware such as 'processor,' 'server,' 'client,' 'computer,' 'GPS device,' or Internet infrastructure does not supply an inventive concept by itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiple holdings state that adding a server/client/processor or placing an idea 'online' or in a 'particular technological environment' (e.g., mobile devices) is insufficient when those elements perform conventional functions. Courts emphasize that generic computer implementation that does not change computer behavior is inadequate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Problem must be rooted in computer technology to save claims
rubrics_metrics.description: To be patent-eligible, claimed solutions should address a problem 'necessarily rooted in computer technology' or provide a technological improvement to computer functioning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims that solve problems that existed before computers or that are 'not necessarily rooted in computer technology' (e.g., adjusting information flow, efficient searching, bookkeeping, data organization) are often held abstract. Where a claim provides necessary technological improvements, courts may find eligibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mere automation of an abstract idea is insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: Automating a known human task using a generic computer does not render the claim patent-eligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts rejected claims that simply told a practitioner to implement the abstract idea with routine computer activity, even if the automation made the task more efficient or less error-prone. 'Mere automation through a generic computer' is not enough.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preemption / risk of monopolization concern
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims should not be so broad as to preempt the abstract idea itself or monopolize fundamental practices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts consider whether the claim would effectively prevent others from using the abstract idea and whether the claim sets meaningful boundaries. Lack of specificity that risks monopolization weighs against eligibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim specificity / sufficient structure required
rubrics_metrics.description: To transform an abstract idea into patentable subject matter, claims must ground the idea in specific structure, unique components, or particularized implementation rather than vague 'rules engines' or general directives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: a 'rules engine' described only as general instructions, or a component that 'can be configured' to perform a function, is insufficient. Claims that fail to describe how components are customized or how they operate do not provide the specificity courts require.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty/nonobviousness does not determine §101 eligibility
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim's novelty or nonobviousness under §§102/103 does not make it patent-eligible under §101.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts repeatedly explain that even if an invention is novel and nonobvious, if it only implements an abstract idea using conventional technology it may still be ineligible under §101.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representative-claim treatment requires proof
rubrics_metrics.description: Dismissing or invalidating multiple patents based on a subset of 'representative' claims is inappropriate unless the moving party demonstrates those claims are truly representative of the rest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts have denied wholesale invalidation where defendants failed to prove that a few representative claims sufficiently stood for all asserted claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Courts can decide eligibility without claim construction
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent-eligibility under §101 may be resolved at the motion to dismiss or judgment stage without formal claim construction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some courts rely on judicial experience and common sense at early stages, especially where parties have not identified claim-construction disputes that would affect the §101 analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Human-performable or mental-step claims are abstract
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims whose steps can be performed by human reasoning, pen-and-paper, or mental processes are likely to be abstract.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include comparing data sets, identifying/recognizing signals, observing/analyzing/monitoring/altering, making lists of possible values and selecting among them, or performing age-old information processing (folders, ledgers, libraries).

rubrics_metrics.name: Limiting claims to a particular technological environment is often insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: Simply stating that an abstract idea is implemented in a mobile, Internet, cloud, or interactive television environment does not necessarily confer eligibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts have held that a technological-environment limitation does not save claims where the implementation uses conventional components and does not solve a computer-specific problem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dependent claims must supply meaningful limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: Dependent claims that add only routine or unspecified limitations (e.g., no details about types, sources, or actions) do not typically provide the inventive concept necessary to overcome §101 rejections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts have found dependent claims unhelpful where they do not specify what is collected, where from, or what specific actions follow a match, or where they merely recite additional generic steps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical concepts and scientific principles can be abstract
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims directed to mathematical concepts, complex math, or scientific calculations are sometimes treated as abstract ideas if they merely apply the math using generic hardware.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: motion-tracking relying on Newtonian principles or inertial navigation mathematics was held abstract when implemented with generic devices without inventive concept.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims must describe how claimed solution improves technology
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts look for recitations showing that the claimed invention provides a concrete technological improvement (e.g., changes how computers operate, optimizes interfaces, new searching/analysis/encryption techniques).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assertions of hypothetical benefits (e.g., massive scale-up, reduced expense, privacy improvements) that are not recited in the claims themselves will not establish eligibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Using longstanding business practices is abstract
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that merely implement traditional business methods, economic strategies, or conventional commercial transactions (coupons, discounts, booking/tracing shipping, intermediated transactions) are treated as abstract ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts cite examples where the claimed systems merely digitize or automate business practices without inventive technological improvements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims framed as information collection/organization are often abstract
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that claim gathering, storing, labeling, normalizing, or organizing data (e.g., containerized data, searchable containers, data normalization, indexing) are frequently deemed abstract absent specific technological improvements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts analogize such claims to libraries, ledgers, folders, time-cards and emphasize that implementing these practices on a computer without specific improvements does not confer eligibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vague 'custom' or 'configured' component language is legally insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: Descriptions that a component is 'custom,' 'configured,' or 'can be configured' without specifying how it differs from conventional components do not provide an inventive concept.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts require description of what the customization is and how it departs from routine implementations; mere labels of 'custom component' are inadequate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims should not be judged solely by the alleged 'genius' of the idea
rubrics_metrics.description: Even clever or creative ideas are not automatically patent-eligible if they claim an abstract idea implemented in a conventional way.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts note that patent law does not grant protection for all 'inspirations of genius' absent the requisite inventive concept and specificity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improvements limited to a particular machine must show meaningful modification
rubrics_metrics.description: Simply limiting an abstract idea to a machine or particular device (e.g., elevator computer, mobile device) does not save the claim unless the limitation meaningfully changes how the machine operates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts reject arguments that tying an idea to a particular machine is dispositive if the claimed machine is a generic computer performing conventional tasks.
